title: Autonomy Vs Consistency
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Jo Castelino, a secondary teacher, asks how much autonomy teachers should have versus how much consistency a school should demand. She starts from her own experience of thriving under a supportive head of department, which let her try visualisers, live drawing and mini-whiteboards that no one else in the department was using. She then tests the question from four seats, the school leader, the novice teacher, the expert teacher and the student, and finds that each sees different costs in too much freedom or too much uniformity. Her working conclusion is that whole-school routines unrelated to subject, such as behaviour management, should be consistent, while subject-shaped strategies like retrieval practice need room for adaptation. The method she lands on is to explain the principles behind a strategy to everyone affected, then ask for consistency in the act of delivery and autonomy in the method. She is candid that the thinking is unfinished and offered as a way to make sense of it.
points: Leaders cannot verify equal effectiveness under full autonomy, but dictating a format for an evidence-backed strategy such as retrieval practice drains its impact, so the principles (the why, when and how) should be made explicit and the implementation left to teachers.
Novice teachers need structure and guidance because, without understanding the reasoning behind a strategy, they construct their own meaning and learn by trial and error.
Expert teachers experience mandated practices that ignore context as a return to being a novice, which breeds frustration.
Students find it exhausting when routines such as where the Do Now goes or what silent means differ lesson to lesson, so behaviour and routine expectations merit whole-school consistency.
The proposed resolution is consistency in the act of delivery and autonomy in the method of delivery, on a sliding scale depending on context.
quotes: Teachers with autonomy thrive. This may seem like a bold statement but I say this because of my own experience.

If all teachers have full autonomy, you cannot be sure everyone’s practice is equally effective unless you observe them often. If you know there is evidence that suggests something is highly effective (eg. incorporating retrieval practice in lessons), then you would want all staff to implement it.

In my opinion, the key here is to make the principles behind something clear to staff so they understand the why, when and how. And then give staff the autonomy to implement the strategy in their lessons.

You know your subject well and, more importantly, you know how to teach your subject. If someone dictates what you should do in the classroom, it can make you feel frustrated and like a novice teacher again. This is much worse when the strategy doesn’t even make sense to use in your classroom.
Imagine being a student who wants to get things right but struggles to because of these variations in practice. Some routines have to be different in different classrooms.

Complete consistency with no thought of context is not helpful but neither is complete autonomy. Some strategies are there to support a school culture. Some are needed to help students build confidence. Some help novice teachers with their practice.
